highlights.quote: A wound is an event in a body. It is not automatically an event between groups.
highlights.judgment: The book's governing distinction, stated early and with real economy; it earns the methodological caution that follows for 15 chapters.

highlights.quote: The first cities did not cure aggression. They gave it offices, rations, walls, formations, and names.
highlights.judgment: Genuinely good closing cadence, but it is also the book's signature move — negate, then supply a five-item noun list — and it recurs to the point of formula.

highlights.quote: A report intended to show military efficiency could therefore turn a human body into a receipt.
highlights.judgment: The strongest single sentence in the book: the thesis about bureaucratised harm compressed into one concrete image.

highlights.quote: the Fatimid Maghreb records, in the material available here, a pattern of frontier coercion
highlights.judgment: A leak of the drafting apparatus into the prose; 'the material available here', 'the surviving account summarized in the evidence' and 'the research note gives a range' all break the historian's voice.

highlights.quote: The grave is a sample, sometimes an unusually grave sample, and samples do not become populations merely because their contents are dramatic.
highlights.judgment: An unintended pun that wrecks an otherwise careful sentence — evidence that the copy-edit pass was uneven.

highlights.quote: It cannot reveal the complete motive of every killer or survivor. It cannot recreate every road not taken.
highlights.judgment: In the final chapter this anaphoric run has lost its grammatical subject across a paragraph break; the strongest rhetorical passage is also the most broken one.

highlights.quote: Someone had to determine the quantity required. Someone had to locate the materials. Someone had to inspect the result.
highlights.judgment: Where specificity fails, the book substitutes an abstract procedural chant; several chapters have one of these placeholder paragraphs.

highlights.quote: Nataruk and Talheim make episode visible; Jebel Sahaba makes recurrence visible; Crow Creek reminds us that similar mortuary forms can occur in societies separated by time and circumstance.
highlights.judgment: Comparative discipline done well — differentiated cases held apart rather than fused into one prehistoric war.

recurringPatterns.pattern: The staged historians' duel: every chapter recruits two named scholars with opposed emphases, weighs them, and issues a verdict, often with the word 'verdict' or 'I agree/I side'. By chapter five the reader can predict the paragraph's arrival.
instances: Parker is right about connection. Black is right about unevenness. I would not resolve the dispute by choosing technology over administration
I therefore side with Kaeuper against any account that treats medieval violence primarily as political disorder.

recurringPatterns.pattern: The concessive negation formula — 'X shows A. It does not show B.' — used as the default paragraph-closer several hundred times across the book. It is the source of both the book's credibility and most of its bloat.
instances: The injury is not only evidence of an act. It is evidence of an interval.
The number of bodies can establish concentration. It cannot establish motive.

recurringPatterns.pattern: One-line paragraphs used as inter-section pivots, isolated for aphoristic weight, usually to hand off from one artifact to the next.
instances: The royal image was a lesson.
A ledger does not travel evenly across a landscape.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Paired antithetical sentences with matched syntax, deployed as the standard rhetorical unit rather than reserved for emphasis.
instances: The raid disrupted a place. The campaign tried to rearrange its future.
A peace agreement is not a human instinct. Neither is a genocide.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Cross-chapter recap of earlier evidence in near-identical wording, so that later chapters re-teach material rather than assume it.
instances: The Barbados Code of 1661 defined enslaved people as “goods and Chattels” and authorized owners extensive powers of punishment, including mutilation and burning alive.
On the Codrington plantations, owned by the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel after Christopher Codrington's bequest in 1710, at least 300 enslaved people were required to work 763 acres.

summary: This is a serious, chronologically ordered global history whose thesis — that aggression is a constant human capacity while institutions decide its scale, targets and meaning — is stated in chapter one, tested against artefacts in every chapter, and re-examined methodologically in chapter fifteen. Its distinctive strength is evidentiary discipline: the book repeatedly refuses to let a wound become a war or a monument become a report, and it names what each source can and cannot carry. The prose is clean, concrete and free of the usual lexical tells; the sourcing is specific (Jebel Sahaba's sixty-one skeletons, Codrington's 763 acres, the Yuan relay's 1,519 stations), and comparisons are held apart rather than flattened. Against that, the book is structurally templated to a degree that becomes visible early: an artefact, a careful reading, a duel between two named historians, a verdict, an aphoristic closer, with 'X shows A; it does not show B' as the reflex sentence. The result is slow reading with heavy redundancy, uniform paragraph shapes and little tonal variation across four hundred pages of argument. A few passages leak the drafting process ('in the material available here', 'the research note gives a range'), and the final chapter contains a paragraph that has lost its grammatical subject — signs that trimming and a close copy-edit are still owed.
